# Maternal prenatal carotenoids and child lung function- exploration of modifying factors

**Authors:** Xueying Zhang; Terryl J. Hartman; Margaret Adgent; Paul Moore; Tebeb Gebretsadik; Marshae Nickelberry; Kaja Z. LeWinn; Qi Zhao; Kecia N. Carroll; Rosalind J. Wright

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Environmental Medicine, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY | 2Institute for Exposomics, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY | 3Jack and Lucy Clark Department of Pediatrics, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY | 4Department of Epidemiology, Rollins School of Public Health, Emory University, Atlanta, GA | 5Department of Health Policy, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN | 6Department of Pediatrics, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN | 7Department of Biostatistics, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN | 8Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Harvard University, Boston, MA | 9Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, University of California, San Francisco, CA | 10Department of Preventive Medicine, College of Medicine, University of Tennessee Health Science Center, Memphis, TN | 11Department of Public Health, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY

## Abstract

While childhood airways outcomes have been associated with prenatal nutrition, few studies examined carotenoids, a group of nutrients with antioxidant properties, or potential modifiers.

In N=677 mother-child dyads enrolled in the CANDLE cohort, we examined associations between prenatal carotenoids (α-carotene, β-carotene, β-cryptoxanthin, lycopene, and zeaxanthin) and child lung function at age 8–9 years. Maternal-child factors that may modify associations were also assessed.

Second trimester plasma carotenoid concentrations were assayed and corrected for cholesterol. Outcomes included forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), forced vital capacity (FVC), and FEV1/FVC z-scores. We used multivariable linear regression to investigate associations between individual carotenoids and lung function z-scores adjusting for covariates. We also examined effect modification by maternal smoking, body mass index, asthma and child sex by including cross-product terms.

We did not detect statistically significant associations between individual carotenoid concentrations and child lung function in main effect models. Modifying effects of prenatal smoking were observed between all five carotenoids and FEV1 (all pinteraction<0.05). For example, a two-fold increase of α-carotene was associated with an increase in FEV1 z-score of 0.45 (95% CI: 0.08, 0.86) among children whose mothers smoked prenatally vs. a 0.01 (−0.08, 0.10) change in children born to women who did not smoke.

A protective association between higher prenatal carotenoid concentrations and FEV1 in middle childhood was observed among children whose mothers smoked during pregnancy.

## Abstract

## INTRODUCTION

Childhood lung function is a determinant of respiratory health and a predictor of morbidity in later life.1 Growing evidence suggests that maternal nutritional exposures during pregnancy, including dietary antioxidants, play a critical role in offspring lung development and respiratory health.2 Several processes, including oxidative stress and inflammation, are widely recognized as mechanisms that may influence the developing lung and immune system.3–5 A group of nutrients with noted antioxidant properties that may play a role in child lung function include provitamin A (e.g., β-carotene, α-carotene, β-cryptoxanthin) and non-provitamin A (e.g. lycopene, zeaxanthin) carotenoids which are naturally occurring compounds abundant in brightly colored fruit and vegetables.6 Findings from in vitro studies and animal models support the role of carotenoids as “scavengers” of pro-oxidants including singlet molecular oxygen and peroxyl radicals, while oral supplementation with carotenoids has been associated with increased antioxidant capability measures compared to controls.7 Regarding epidemiologic studies, higher levels of serum carotenoids have been associated with decreased asthma in a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults.8 Higher intake and serum levels were positively associated with lung function outcomes in adult samples.3 In addition, serum levels of specific carotenoids were inversely associated with decline in FEV1 in adults.9, 10

The investigation of associations of prenatal antioxidants and child respiratory and atopic disease outcomes is an active area of research,11, 12 However the literature around prenatal carotenoids and child lung function is less extensive, although one study found a significant increasing trend between carotene intake and FEV1.12 In addition, previous studies have found differences in the association between other prenatal nutritional exposures and child asthma by maternal asthma history and child sex13 and these exposures may also modify associations between prenatal carotenoids and child lung function. Maternal obesity and smoking during pregnancy are associated with oxidative stress and with lower carotenoid levels even after adjusting for dietary intake14 and whether these conditions modify the association between prenatal carotenoids and child lung function is of interest.

In dyads enrolled in the Conditions Affecting Neurocognitive Development and Learning in Early childhood (CANDLE) cohort, we investigated the association between five carotenoids (α-carotene, β-carotene, β-cryptoxanthin, lycopene, and zeaxanthin) measured from maternal 2nd trimester plasma and child lung function outcomes at 8–9-years of age. We hypothesized that higher carotenoid levels during pregnancy would be associated with better lung function outcomes in children. Furthermore, we investigated whether maternal asthma, obesity, and smoking during pregnancy, or child sex modified the association between prenatal carotenoid concentrations and child lung function and explored three-way interactions with child sex.

## METHODS

### Study participants

CANDLE is a pregnancy cohort established to investigate the association of pre-and postnatal exposures on child neurocognitive development and learning which expanded to include phenotyping of child respiratory outcomes.13, 15 The CANDLE team at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center (UTHSC) enrolled 1,503 pregnant women, December 2006 to June 2011, who met eligibility: Shelby County resident, age between 16 and 40 years, and had a low-risk singleton pregnancy.15 Women 18 years and older provided informed consent for themselves and children; for those less than 18 years of age the legally authorized representative provided consent and the women provided assent. Children provided assent at the 8–9 year study visit, which measured the spirometry and anthropometric data used in this analysis.

Our study included dyads with complete data for both maternal carotenoids and child spirometry outcomes. Spirometry measures were over-read by the study pediatric pulmonologist; tests with unacceptable efforts were excluded (N=60). Overall, 739 children had spirometry data that met American Thoracic Society (ATS)16 criteria. We excluded dyads with infants <32 week estimated gestational age (n=13) as very or extremely preterm infants have higher prevalence of prematurity-associated lung conditions. Additionally, 31 dyads were excluded due to missing carotenoid data. Non-Black or -White dyads were excluded (n=6) due to small sample size. An additional 12 dyads were excluded due to missing covariates. Our final analysis included 677 dyads. The study was approved by UTHSC and the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai Institutional Review Boards.

### Primary outcomes: lung function z-scores

Staff completed spirometry at the child age 8–9 visit, using established protocols outlined by ATS.16, 17 Assessments were conducted using a portable MedGraphicsTM PC-based USB spirometer, which generated real-time flow-volume plots. Flow measurements were obtained using a heated screen pneumotachograph, featuring a flow range of 0±20 l/s and an accuracy within 0.2 to 12 l/s ±2%. Volume measurements were achieved through digital integration. We obtained forced vital capacity (FVC, liters) and forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1, liters). The FEV1/FVC ratio was calculated. Raw FEV1 and FVC values were transformed into z-scores using the race-neutral reference equations established by the Global Lung Function Initiative (GLI).18

### Maternal prenatal carotenoids and cholesterol biomarkers

Second trimester plasma carotenoids (α-carotene, β-carotene, β-cryptoxanthin, lycopene, and zeaxanthin) were analyzed at the Molecular Epidemiology and Biomarker Research Laboratory at the University of Minnesota using an established extraction method.19 In brief, carotenoids were extracted from plasma and analyzed using high-performance liquid chromatography, and measured values were calibrated based on the method in Craft et al.20 Lipids are the main carotenoid carriers and play an important role in carotenoid absorption and bioavailability.21 A number of lipid-soluble nutrients, including carotenoids, are transported by lipoproteins, and their concentrations are related to the concentration of cholesterol in the blood. Thus, it has been recommended that when blood concentrations of lipid soluble nutrients are used as indicators of intake they should be adjusted for blood cholesterol.22 Therefore, raw concentrations (μg/dl) of carotenoids were normalized by calculating their ratios against corresponding blood cholesterol concentrations (mg/dl).23 Total cholesterol was measured on a Roche COBAS 8000 chemistry analyzer.

### Covariates

Covariates collected at enrollment included self-reported maternal race and ethnicity (non-Hispanic Black, non-Hispanic White, or Hispanic), highest educational attainment (< high school, high school, or ≥college), age (years), asthma history (yes, no), pre-pregnancy Body Mass Index (BMI, weight in kilograms/meters squared) characterized as healthy (< 25), overweight (≥25 to <30), or obese (≥ 30), parity (0, 1, >1 prior live births), and self-reported smoking during pregnancy (yes or no). Child sex (female, male) and season of birth (Summer, Spring, Fall, Winter) were obtained at delivery. Child age and height were assessed at spirometry measurement.

### Statistical Analyses

Descriptive statistics were estimated for carotenoid levels, lung function outcomes (FEV1, FVC, and FEV1/FVC z-scores), and the characteristics of mothers. We summarized raw concentrations of carotenoids using median and interquartile range (IQR) due to the skewness. We summarized other continuous variables using means and standard deviations (SD) and present categorical variables as counts and percentages. We examined CANDLE participants who completed spirometry tests, the study sample, and those excluded (see Table S1).

Prior to conducting regression analyses, raw carotenoid concentrations (μg/dl) were normalized by calculating their ratios against corresponding blood cholesterol concentrations (mg/dl). Furthermore, we applied a logarithm base 2 transformation to carotenoid/cholesterol ratios (herein “carotenoid concentrations”) for normalization. We assessed the normality of raw concentrations, carotenoid/cholesterol ratios, log2-transformed ratios, and the distribution of outcome variables (FEV1, FVC, and FEV1/FVC z-scores) by generating histograms (see Supplementary Document, Figure S1–S2). After applying the log2 transformation, the distributions of carotenoids shifted from skewed to approximately normal, particularly for α-carotene and β-carotene.

We assessed the association between carotenoids and child lung function outcomes (FEV1, FVC, and FEV1/FVC z-scores) in separate multivariable linear regression models adjusting for maternal race, education, asthma history, pre-pregnancy BMI, smoking status, child sex, age, and height. Race is a sociopolitical construct and not based on biology or genetic ancestry, therefore we adjusted for maternal race as it may represent differences related to individual or structural racism or other structural inequities in particular as related to maternal nutritional status and child asthma outcomes.24 Since we applied a logarithm base 2 transformation to the carotenoid/cholesterol ratio, the estimated coefficients denoting the association between carotenoid concentrations and lung function z-scores as the average change in z-score associated with a two-fold increase in carotenoid concentrations (μg/mg cholesterol). We performed simple model diagnosis by examining the normality of residuals (see Supplementary Figure S3). Additionally, we performed a sensitivity analysis by using log 2 of raw carotenoid concentrations (see Supplementary Figure S4 & S5). Next, we examined modifying effects of maternal asthma history, pre-pregnancy BMI, and smoking status and child sex on associations between carotenoids and child lung function outcome. We included interaction terms in the regression models, where each carotenoid concentration was multiplied by the respective effect modifiers (e.g., maternal asthma history × pre-pregnancy BMI). To explore potential three-way interactions, we conducted additional analyses that assessed how child sex interacted with maternal smoking, BMI category, or asthma history. These interactions were modeled by incorporating cross-product terms of the three variables in the regression models.

## RESULTS

Table 1 provides an overview of the characteristics and raw concentrations of carotenoids for study dyads. The majority of women were non-Hispanic Black (65.6%), followed by non-Hispanic White (32.8%). Overall, 55.8% of women had high school as the highest level of educational attainment and 12.6% reported having asthma. Approximately 8.6% of women reported smoking during pregnancy. Women with higher educational attainment had higher concentrations of all five study carotenoids, and women who did not smoke during pregnancy or had a healthy BMI had elevated carotenoid levels compared to reference groups.

Table 2 demonstrates bivariate associations of lung function outcomes (FEV1, FVC, and FEV1/FVC z-scores) and maternal characteristics. Children born to women with higher levels of educational attainment or of White race had higher FEV1 and FVC z-scores compared to their respective comparison groups. No other statistically significant differences were observed when comparing lung function outcomes across other maternal characteristics subgroups.

Figure 1 illustrates the multivariable associations between prenatal carotenoid concentrations and child lung function outcomes z-scores. No significant associations were observed. A borderline association was detected between β-carotene and FVC z-score, with the 95% confidence interval (CI) approaching significance (coefficient: 0.09, 95% CI: −0.001, 0.17).

Figure 2 presents the associations between prenatal carotenoid concentrations and lung function z-scores, stratified by maternal smoking status. In addition, we tested interaction using cross-product terms (see Supplementary Table S2). Across all five carotenoid models, significant interactions were detected (all pint< 0.05). A two-fold increase of α-carotene, β-carotene, β-cryptoxanthin, lycopene and zeaxanthin concentrations was respectively associated with an average change in child FEV1 z-score of 0.45 (95% CI: 0.08, 0.83), 0.32 (0.08, 0.57), 0.98 (0.28, 1.58), 0.46 (0.00, 0.90), and 1.09 (0.34, 1.92) in dyads with a history of maternal smoking during pregnancy, and 0.01 (−0.08, 0.10), 0.04 (−0.04, 0.13), −0.13 (−0.34, 0.07), −0.05 (−0.18, 0.09), and −0.01 (−0.25, 0.25) in dyads without maternal smoking. We found that a two-fold increase in zeaxanthin concentration was associated with 0.87 (0.14, 1.65) and 0.07 (−0.16, 0.31) change in child FVC z-scores in women with and without a history of smoking during pregnancy, respectively (pint=0.04). We did not detect interaction by maternal smoking with child FVC z-scores in associations with other carotenoids. A two-fold increase in lycopene was associated with 0.77 (0.22, 1.38) and −0.03 (−0.21, 0.15) change in FEV1/FVC z-scores in children born to women with and without a history of smoking during pregnancy, respectively (pint = 0.005); effect modification was also found for α-carotene and FEV1/FVC z-scores (pint = 0.02). In general, associations between prenatal carotenoids, maternal smoking, and child lung function outcomes did not vary by child sex (see Supplementary Figure S6 and Supplementary Table S2) although higher prenatal β-carotene concentrations were associated with 0.48 (0.002, 0.96) higher FEV1/FVC z-scores only in males with smoking mothers (3-way pint=0.02).

We did not detect evidence of effect modification by child sex between the association of individual carotenoids and child lung function outcomes (all pint> 0.23, See Supplementary Table S2 for exact p-values) data not shown. We also did not detect robust evidence of effect modification in the association between prenatal carotenoids and child lung function by maternal pre-pregnancy BMI, with the exception of β-cryptoxanthin and FEV1, which was not in a consistent direction across the BMI categories from “healthy” to “obese” (see Supplementary Figure S7 and Supplementary Table S2). There was evidence of effect modification by child sex in three-way interactions; however, a consistent pattern was not noted (see Supplementary Figure S8 and Supplementary Table S2) across outcomes or child sex. Lastly, there was limited evidence of effect modification by maternal asthma and prenatal carotenoid concentrations and lung function outcomes, except higher prenatal lycopene levels were associated with decreased FEV1 (pint=0.046) and FVC (pint=0.047) in dyads with a mother with asthma but not without asthma (see Supplementary Figure S9 and Supplementary Table S2). Effect modification was not detected in three-way interactions including child sex (all pint ≥0.1) (see Supplementary Figure S10 and Supplementary Table S2).

## DISCUSSION

We investigated the association between maternal prenatal carotenoid concentrations during pregnancy and child lung function in a racially diverse cohort of mother-child dyads. In overall models, we did not detect associations apart from a suggested positive association between β-carotene and FVC. In analyses, maternal smoking during pregnancy modified the association between carotenoid concentrations and child lung function. For dyads in which a woman reported smoking during pregnancy, higher concentrations of each individual carotenoid were associated with higher FEV1 in children; an association not seen in children of women who did not smoke during pregnancy. We did not detect a similar pattern of effect modification by maternal pre-pregnancy BMI or asthma history or child sex.

Previous investigations have found inconsistent associations between maternal prenatal intake of carotenoids and child lung function or asthma and atopic disease outcomes. In the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) birth cohort study,12 that measured dietary intake during pregnancy by Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ), children of women within the highest quartile of carotenoid intake had higher FEV1 and FVC than those in the lowest, but associations were attenuated after covariate adjustment. Additional studies have investigated prenatal carotenoid intake or biomarker concentrations and child respiratory or atopic disease outcomes. In the Project Viva cohort, Sordillo et al.25 did not detect associations between prenatal β-carotene intake, measured using semiquantitative FFQ and characterized as z-score, and asthma and atopic disease outcomes in early adolescence. In the Polish Mother and Child Cohort Study, Bobrowska-Korzeniowska et al.26 did not detect associations between cord blood β-carotene concentrations and child respiratory and atopic disease outcomes for children aged 7–9 years old.

Of some relevance, provitamin A carotenoids (e.g. β-carotene, α-carotene, β-cryptoxanthin) can be converted to vitamin A and there have been several investigations of vitamin A and child respiratory conditions in study populations with a high prevalence of vitamin A deficiency.27 In follow-up of a cohort of Nepali children whose mothers participated in a placebo-controlled, cluster randomized trial of vitamin A or β-carotene supplementation prior to, during and after pregnancy,27 vitamin A supplementation was linked to higher FEV1 and FVC in children aged 9 to 13 years compared to placebo; β-carotene supplementation was associated with child lung function outcomes similar to placebo.

Several epidemiologic studies explored whether maternal smoking during pregnancy modified the association between maternal nutritional exposures and offspring lung function with inconclusive results. An investigation (Bédard et al.28) in the ALSPAC cohort detected weak positive associations between higher Mediterranean diet score and child forced expiratory flow at 25–75% of forced vital capacity (FEF25–75%), however they did not detect effect modification by maternal smoking status. In their another investigation, Bédard et al.12 did not detect effect modification by maternal smoking in the association between prenatal carotenoid intake and child asthma and lung function outcomes. In a RCT that included women who smoked during pregnancy, McEvoy et al.29 found that vitamin C supplementation was associated with improved lung function during infancy with follow-up into early childhood demonstrating persistent protective effects. A review study30 on diet and childhood asthma and allergies did not find evidence of a significant modifying effect of maternal smoking in the included studies. Nevertheless, our findings support consideration of maternal smoking during pregnancy as an effect modifier in investigations of prenatal carotenoid exposures and child asthma. This may be attributed to the increased statistical power in our study which used measured carotenoid biomarkers during pregnancy which assess the exposure of interest more precisely and continuous lung function z-scores, whereas previous studies relied on FFQ data that is more vulnerable to measurement error and reduced precision or categorical outcomes.

There are several potential mechanisms through which prenatal carotenoid concentrations may influence child lung function.31–33 Carotenoids are known for their capacity to mitigate oxidative stress and reduce inflammation.31 Higher levels of maternal carotenoids may protect against oxidative damage, thus positively influencing lung development in utero.32 Additionally, infant lung development differentiation begins in early gestation and continues throughout gestation and postnatally,34 and provitamin A carotenoids contribute to formation of retinoic acid, a key signaling molecule involved in multiple aspects of lung development that influence airways function.35 Furthermore, it is possible that maternal carotenoids confer epigenetic modifications33 that influence the expression of genes crucial for lung development and function. Direct effects of oxidative stress and associated inflammation as well as epigenetic modulation may contribute to the modifying effects of maternal smoking observed in our study.36 In some studies, women who smoked during pregnancy had evidence of higher markers of oxidative stress during pregnancy, in cord blood or in infant biomarkers as well as reduced antioxidant capacity.37, 38 Oxidative stress caused by cigarette smoking may consume antioxidant micronutrients.38 In addition, smoking might decrease absorption of micronutrients due to inflammatory responses in the intestine.39 Maternal smoking has been associated with alterations in the methylation patterns of several CpG sites,40 including some with key roles in respiratory development. Smoking during pregnancy is associated with many adverse conditions during the perinatal period as well as later in childhood41 and all pregnant individuals should be informed of risks and smoking cessation of tobacco products should be advised.41 As smoking cessation is unsuccessful in over 40% of pregnant individuals who smoke before pregnancy, maternal nutritional status may play a role in mitigating prenatal effects of smoking when cessation is not achieved, as shown in one randomized controlled trial.29, 41

Maternal obesity and maternal asthma have both been recognized as potential effect modifiers in the association between maternal prenatal nutritional exposures and subsequent respiratory outcomes,13, 30 as both obesity and asthma are sources of cumulative oxidative stress.42 However, we did not find a consistent effect modification pattern of these two maternal characteristics. These null findings could be attributed to several reasons. In the overall population, maternal BMI may not be strongly associated with elevated oxidative stress. Furthermore, using a carotenoid-to-cholesterol ratio could potentially attenuate the relationship between carotenoid exposure and BMI. Given the relatively small sample size of women with asthma (n=85), our results may be subject to some uncertainty. It is possible that lycopene metabolism among women with asthma is altered possibly due to the condition or medications used to treat the condition thereby influencing lycopene’s role in counteracting oxidative stress. These results should be interpreted cautiously, and the association assessed in studies that include larger numbers of women with asthma.

Our inclusion of carotenoid biomarkers and investigation of individual carotenoids are strengths and provide insight into how specific carotenoids may influence childhood lung function. Participants were not included based on carotenoid deficiency further enhancing the generalizability and the potential to inform future investigations. Although, assessment of prenatal carotenoid concentrations relied on measurements taken at a single time point, carotenoid concentrations have been shown to be consistent over time, correlated with fruit and vegetable intake,43 and compared to self-reported nutritional data are less prone to misclassification in observational studies.22

Regarding limitations, as in all observational studies there may be unmeasured confounders. Although we adjusted for a number of important confounders that were related to both maternal carotenoid concentrations and child lung function, it is possible that residual confounding and unmeasured dietary (e.g., unmeasured and potentially correlated antioxidant biomarkers) or other lifestyle exposures influenced our observed associations.44 The subgroup of women who reported smoking was relatively small and self-reported smoking may be subject to non-differential misclassification. Regarding multiplicity correction, we did not perform such correction as we had taken the following considerations. First, our three outcome variables (FEV1, FVC, and FEV1/FVC z-scores) are correlated. In such cases, treating each outcome as an independent model and performing multiplicity correction can lead to overly conservative corrections, potentially missing non-spurious or actual effects.45 Second, we presented all p-values of interactions tested in supplement Table S2, so that the reader has complete data and interprets the results comprehensively. There were some limitations related to data availability. We were not able to include measures of postnatal child diet which may influence child lung function. The maternal asthma variable used in our analysis did not distinguish between atopic and non-atopic asthma phenotypes. We are not able to conduct separate analysis based on the subtypes of asthma. This work supports future investigations with larger sample sizes to further investigate findings.

## Conclusion

Our investigation of individual carotenoids and child asthma found that higher levels of both prenatal provitamin and non-provitamin carotenoids were associated with higher FEV1 in mid-childhood in children of women who smoked during pregnancy, but not among children of women who did not smoke. Further research is needed to elucidate the mechanisms underlying findings and may inform potential interventions, particularly for women who are not able to achieve smoking cessation during pregnancy.
